t: Maximum Total Reward Using Operations I
o:
## Understanding the problem

Starting from x = 0, repeatedly pick an unused value v; you may add it only if v > x. Maximize the final x.

Example 1 `[1,1,3,3]`: take 1 (x=1), then 3 (x=4) → 4. Taking both 3s is impossible since after x=3 the second 3 fails `3 > 3`. Example 2 `[1,6,4,3,2]`: 1 → 4 → 6 gives 11.

Key observation: taking values in increasing order is optimal (any achievable set can be reordered increasingly and remains valid, since each added value exceeds the sum of smaller chosen ones). Also, the final total is always less than 2·max(rewardValues) ≤ 4000, because the last added value v satisfies previous_total < v, so total < 2v ≤ 4000. That bounds a subset-sum-style DP over sums up to 4000 with n ≤ 2000 — about 8 million transitions.
k: Sort the values; any optimal selection can be taken in increasing order, so order doesn't restrict us.
The answer never reaches 2·max(value), capping the DP sum dimension at 4000.
dp[s] = true iff total s is achievable; when processing value v (sorted), we may extend any achievable s < v to s + v.

a.n: Approach 1: Subset-sum boolean DP on sorted values
a.i: After sorting, process values one at a time and maintain the set of achievable totals. Value v can extend exactly those achievable totals strictly below v. Iterating sums downward prevents reusing v within the same step. The answer is the maximum achievable total.
s: Initialize dp[0] = true; iterate v in sorted order, and for s from (current max) down to 0: if dp[s] and s < v, set dp[s+v] = true.
Track and return the largest s with dp[s] true.
a.t: O(n log n + n·S) with S ≤ 4000 — about 8·10⁶ operations for n = 2000.

a.i: Represent the achievable-sum set as one big integer where bit s means 'sum s achievable'. Processing value v: take the bits below v (`mask & ((1<<v)-1)`), shift them left by v, and OR into the mask. This performs a whole DP layer transition in a handful of word-level operations — dramatically faster in practice.
s: Sort values; maintain Python int / C++ bitset / JS BigInt `mask`, initially 1 (bit 0 set).
Answer = highest set bit position of mask.
a.t: O(n·S/w) word operations — near-instant for S = 4000.

## Wrap-up

Lead with the boolean DP (easy to explain and prove), then mention the bitset trick as the optimization interviewers love. Pitfalls: forgetting to sort (order matters for correctness of the '< v' check), iterating sums upward (reusing v), and allocating the DP only up to max(values) instead of 2·max(values). Follow-up: the harder version (n up to 5·10⁴) requires divide-and-conquer over the bitset trick.
